purpose: The Server's execution context, replayed. Each case carries the op (without the schema wrapper) and the answer the kernel must give: the parsed answer, or {"error": "<the exact Err string>"} when the request itself is malformed. ds-web replays the same file through the vendored WASM, so no rule about who may see, admit, keep, queue or recover a project's work can be true on one host and not another.
source: ds-web/docs/project-and-instance-isolation-contract.md (One verified context per operation; Server jobs and multiple clients; Concurrency and capacity; acceptance items 2, 5, 6, 7, 8), 2026-09-12, under the owner's boundary ruling of the same day: the Server is the desktop's core and holds no project directory, so admission is the connection, the named project and the key. Third pass, same day: a project id is one path segment that no filesystem reads as a drive, a device or a stream, a per-project limit must divide the host limit it shares, and the cross-project half of scope_mismatch_for_key is gone because a durable id digests the project.
note: Re-record expected with DS_EXECUTION_CONTEXT_CASES_WRITE=1 cargo test --test execution_context_cases after a deliberate rule change, and say why in the commit.

cases.why: An explicitly named project is the whole happy path: the record is stamped from the authenticated connection and the name the owner gave, not from anything the caller asserted about itself.
A legacy saved-project field is rejected as an unknown input, so no host can silently substitute an active selection.

expected.error: invalid execution context request: unknown field `saved_project`, expected one of `now_ms`, `principal`, `client`, `operation`, `job_id`, `idempotency_key`, `input_sha256`, `requested_project`, `sealed_project`, `existing` at line 1 column 443

cases.why: An explicit project names the request without consulting any saved selection or process-wide active project.
A sealed Solar submission names its own project, so admission needs no saved selection or active host project.
Naming the same project the sealed bytes name is not a conflict; it is the ordinary explicit Solar submission and it admits.
A Solar submit whose sealed input was prepared for one project while the caller names another is refused scope_mismatch, and the refusal names only the project the caller already knows.

refusal.message: this request is for project-b, but its sealed input was prepared for another project; submit it without naming a project, or prepare an input for project-b

cases.why: No requested project, no saved default and no sealed input means there is nothing to record; the kernel refuses rather than inventing one from process state.

refusal.message: no project was named for this request; pass --project or submit sealed input that names its project

cases.why: The same key, project, operation and input bytes is an idempotent resubmit: the context already admitted comes back unchanged, so a retry never creates a second scope or re-stamps the admission time.

The durable job id digests the project as well as the owner, lane and key, so the same key in two projects is two jobs and never reaches this refusal; what a key still cannot do is name a second operation inside its own project, where the id would collide.

refusal.message: that idempotency key already names another project or operation; submit this under a key of its own

cases.why: Same key, same project, different bytes: the caller is trying to overwrite an existing result, which is refused rather than silently accepted or silently reused.

refusal.message: that idempotency key was admitted with different input bytes; resubmit the bytes it was admitted with, or use a new key for these

cases.why: A stored record for this key that belongs to another account is a fence, not a reuse: the Server never lets one principal continue another's admitted work.

cases.why: now_ms is an input so the decision is pure; a host that forgets it has a bug, and a bug is a hard error rather than something to relay to a client.

expected.error: admission needs the host's clock in now_ms

cases.why: Report generation for a second project is the overlapping work the contract demands, so it carries a context of its own exactly like Solar does.
A layer read is an operation too: its request id is its job id and its digest binds the exact request, so status and visibility work the same way for reads.
A layer write against an explicitly named project proves /v1/layers is admitted through the same owner as compute, not through a process-wide selection.
Kernel f4754a2 adds sync_recovery for fenced native recovery of retained publications; it retains the explicitly named project and connection identity just like every admitted operation.
Transformer processing carries no project inside its request by design, which is exactly why an admitted context must be given one by the caller that submits it.
Tile generation is a first-class local compute operation, so its durable execution context must be admitted and project-isolated by the same closed vocabulary as every other server job.
The account that admitted the work sees it without narrowing to a project: reconnection recovers a caller's jobs by stable id, not by whatever is selected now.
Narrowing a listing to the job's own project is the ordinary per-project query and stays visible.
install_id is recorded for provenance but is never a visibility fence, so the same account reconnecting from another machine still recovers its own durable work.
Another account asking about a known id gets the same three words an unknown id gets, so an id leaked out of a log discloses nothing about who owns it.

cases.why: A retry re-runs the same admitted work; it may not silently re-scope it to whatever project is selected at retry time. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.

After a Server restart the queue is reopened from durable rows, and reopening is not re-admission: the context is exactly the one stored. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.
A worker claiming a job inherits the job's context; the worker's own environment contributes nothing to it. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.

Publication is where a wrong project would actually write into someone else's store, so the context it publishes under is the admitted one. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.
Cancellation is an authorized action on a job, not a context change; the record it acts on is unchanged. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.
The identity function still refuses what is not a context: a row damaged on disk is named rather than carried forward into an effect.

cases.why: An idle host admits work; capacity is a bound on saturation, not a gate every request must argue with.
A full running pool never refuses a submission: the job queues. Confusing 'no free worker' with 'no room' would drop admitted work.
One project saturating its own queue is refused with typed guidance instead of unbounded allocation, and the guidance grows with the work already waiting.

refusal.message: this project already has 3 of 3 operations waiting

cases.why: The point of a per-project bound: while A is saturated, B is admitted normally. A long Solar run must leave room for printing.
Global saturation refuses everyone, including a project with nothing queued, and names only counts and limits — never another project.

refusal.message: the server queue is full (8 of 8 waiting)

cases.why: A project may exceed its running share while nothing else is waiting: the machine is used, not idled to defend a share nobody wants.
The fairness rule itself: the moment another project has queued work, a project already at its share stops taking new slots.

refusal.message: this project holds 2 of 2 running slots while other projects are waiting

cases.why: The project that was waiting claims freely, so fairness actually moves work rather than merely blocking the other one.

Two projects both at their share and both with work waiting must not refuse each other: that would idle every free worker while both have work. The share yields only to a waiting project that is under its own share and could take the slot; here none is, so queue order decides.

The same pool with a third project waiting under its share: both projects at their share now yield, and the retry guidance counts only the work that can actually go first, never the waiting work of projects that could not take the slot either.

refusal.message: this project holds 2 of 2 running slots while other projects are waiting

cases.why: Every worker busy refuses the claim globally, whichever project asks, with retry guidance derived from the queue rather than from a clock.

refusal.message: every worker is busy (4 of 4 running)

cases.why: A share equal to the worker pool is no share at all: the first project to arrive may hold every worker while a second waits, which is the one thing the share exists to prevent, so the configuration is refused as the host's own bug.

expected.error: capacity limit per_project_running is 4 and global_running is 4: a share must be smaller than the pool it divides, or one project holds the whole host while another waits; only a single-slot host (global_running 1) has no share, and there per_project_running must be 1

cases.why: A share larger than the pool says even less than one equal to it; both are refused by the same rule, and the message names both numbers so an operator can read the fix off it.

expected.error: capacity limit per_project_running is 5 and global_running is 4: a share must be smaller than the pool it divides, or one project holds the whole host while another waits; only a single-slot host (global_running 1) has no share, and there per_project_running must be 1

cases.why: The queue has the same invariant as the pool: a per-project queue bound equal to the global one lets one project fill the whole queue and leaves a second project nowhere to wait.

expected.error: capacity limit per_project_queued is 8 and global_queued is 8: a share must be smaller than the pool it divides, or one project holds the whole host while another waits; only a single-slot host (global_queued 1) has no share, and there per_project_queued must be 1

cases.why: The smallest rented VM: one worker, one slot, and nothing to divide. Its share must be exactly one because whatever runs holds the machine, so this configuration is admitted rather than refused as an unfair one.
Having no share is not having no bound: the one slot of a single-worker host is full while it runs, and the second project is told so with the global scope and retry guidance.

refusal.message: every worker is busy (1 of 1 running)

cases.why: A pool of one with a share of two is a configuration that promises a slot the host does not have; the single-slot exception admits one share of one, never more.

cases.why: Limits are the host's own configuration, so a zero limit is a host bug and a hard error, never a typed refusal relayed to a client.
The census is the store's own reading of its rows, so a project id in it that is not one segment means the host wrote one it should never have admitted: a hard fault, never a client refusal.
